analysis.one_liner: Grants police officers nationwide federal due-process protections during misconduct investigations, including notice before questioning and closed disciplinary hearings.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote; it sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee from May 2001 until that Congress ended in January 2003, despite 21 bipartisan cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every state and local police agency to follow detailed federal procedures when investigating or disciplining an officer: 24-hour advance notice before questioning, a right to counsel, recorded interviews, an independent hearing before any discipline, strict time limits on filing charges, and limits on what can go into an officer's personnel file. It would also force states to adopt these protections and override weaker state rules. Alongside these officer protections, it requires agencies to accept outside written complaints, post the forms publicly, and notify complainants in writing of the outcome.
analysis.who_benefits: Law enforcement officers facing internal investigations and the unions that represent them. The bill creates a federal floor of due-process rights in misconduct cases — advance notice of questioning, an attorney or union representative at every questioning session, an independent hearing before any discipline, a cap on penalties, and protections for personnel records. It also lets officers engage in political activity and run for office without resigning.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every agency to adopt a written complaint procedure that accepts complaints from people outside the department, provides public access to forms, and requires written notice of the disposition to the complainant.

Gives officers under investigation a set of procedural rights: notification of the investigation 24 hours before questioning, the right to counsel or a union representative during all questioning, questioning at reasonable hours, a full recording of the session, and no compelled lie detector test.

Bars any discipline unless an independent hearing officer or board finds the officer violated the law, requires the agency to hand over its investigative file before the hearing, and forbids the agency from imposing a penalty greater than the hearing officer's recommendation.

Restricts what adverse material may be kept in an officer's personnel record unless the officer has reviewed and commented on it, and erases references to charges where the officer was found not guilty.
Protects officers' ability to engage in political activity off duty and to run for or hold elective office without resigning, unless the roles conflict.

analysis.who_pays: People who file complaints against officers. Investigations cannot begin questioning until 24 hours after the officer is notified, charges generally must be filed within 90 days of the start of an investigation or one year after the agency knew of the alleged violation, and disciplinary hearings are closed to the public unless the officer opens them. State and local agencies lose management flexibility, and their taxpayers bear the cost of the mandated hearing infrastructure.

drawbacks.text: The 24-hour notice requirement gives an officer under investigation a full day of warning before any questioning, which accountability advocates have long argued lets officers coordinate accounts in the close-knit setting of a police department.
Short filing deadlines — generally 90 days from the start of an investigation or one year from when the agency should have known — could time-bar disciplinary charges on slower-moving allegations.
Hearings are closed to the public by default unless the accused officer requests otherwise, and the agency cannot impose any penalty greater than the independent hearing officer or board recommends.

The bill preempts state and local laws that give officers less protection than this federal floor, potentially overriding stricter state accountability rules, and takes effect up to two years after enactment.
Restrictions on adverse material in personnel files and on possession of it by the agency could limit how departments use complaint histories in promotion and staffing decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is not one-sided: the written complaint procedure with public forms and written notice to complainants gives the public a clearer channel than many departments offered in 2001. But the weight of the bill runs the other way. Every core provision — advance notice, counsel at questioning, independent hearings, penalty caps, closed hearings, filing deadlines, and personnel-file limits — reduces management's ability to investigate and punish officers, and it would apply to every state and local department in the country. An honest supporter would concede that the deadline and notice provisions are the parts most likely to let misconduct go unpunished.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Crime Subcommittee, where it sat with no markup, no vote, and no further action for the rest of the 107th Congress.

narrative.text: Representative Jim Ramstad of Minnesota introduced the bill on April 26, 2001, joined by Representative Tom Davis of Virginia.
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced.
On May 9, 2001, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Crime.
That referral was the last action of any kind; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
The bill drew 21 cosponsors from both parties — 9 Republicans and 12 Democrats — but that support never translated into committee action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police departments' management and complainants are no worse off, because the existing rules stayed in place; the officers' unions and their members gained nothing from the bill's death, while accountability advocates avoided a federal override of state discipline rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police accountability advocates and department management

for.name: Rep. Tom Davis
for.what_they_did: Joined Ramstad in introducing the bill.

for.name: Fraternal Order of Police
for.what_they_did: Has long lobbied Congress for a national law enforcement officer bill of rights of this kind.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Chair F. James Sensenbrenner)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote; after referring the bill to its Crime Subcommittee, the committee took no further action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan and roughly proportional to the House: 9 of 223 Republicans and 12 of 208 Democrats signed on, and no recorded opposition appears in the action history — the bill simply died without a vote.

industries.note: The bill would make a union-backed officer bill of rights the national legal floor, locking in advance notice of questioning, independent hearings, penalty caps, and personnel-file protections in every state and local department. For ordinary people, the same procedures raise the cost of holding an officer accountable: slower investigations, time-barred charges, and closed hearings.

industries.industry: State and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: Agencies would lose management flexibility — no questioning before 24-hour notice, mandatory independent hearings, capped penalties, and limits on personnel records — and taxpayers would fund the required hearing infrastructure. Agency discipline is the main tool the public has for police accountability, so management's interest here runs alongside the public's.
